imageInfo.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan mosaicist; photographed by Myrabella
imageInfo.date: 13th century, usually dated to about 1261; photographed 8 November 2012
imageInfo.source: Hagia Sophia, Istanbul, via Wikimedia Commons
imageInfo.note: A genuine Byzantine mosaic, photographed in place. This is the central figure of a three-part Deesis in which the Virgin and John the Baptist turn towards Christ in intercession; the lower part of the panel has been lost, and the white areas are bare plaster where the tesserae are gone. The usual dating places it shortly after 1261, when the Byzantines recovered their capital from the Latin regime installed in 1204, though some scholars argue for a date during the Latin occupation itself. The modelling of the face, built from tiny graded tesserae rather than flat blocks of colour, is the standard example of what late Byzantine mosaicists could do. Photograph released into the public domain.

summary: The Byzantines were the Greek-speaking Orthodox population of the eastern Roman Empire, who called themselves Rhomaioi — Romans — for the whole of the Middle Ages and never once called themselves Byzantine.
overview: A people whose own name for themselves was taken from them twice: by western writers who insisted on calling them Greeks, and by a German scholar in 1557 who gave them the label they are still filed under.
knownFor: Called themselves Rhomaioi, Romans, without qualification, until 1453 and after.
Ran Roman law in Greek, from Justinian's Corpus to the Basilika of the ninth century.
Tore themselves apart over religious images for more than a century, twice.
Exported Orthodoxy, Cyrillic letters and an imperial model across the Slavic world.
Preserved and taught the classical Greek literature that survives today.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: The people this archive files as Byzantines were the population of the eastern Roman Empire: Greek in speech, Orthodox in religion, Roman in law and in their own understanding of who they were. Their state ran from Constantinople and outlasted the western empire by nearly a thousand years.

They were not a nation in the modern sense and never became one. Being a Rhomaios was a matter of religion, language and allegiance rather than descent, and an Armenian general, a Cappadocian farmer and a Slav settled in Thrace could all be Romans on the same terms.
The empire they ran — its emperors, dynasties, wars and its end in 1453 — is the subject of the Byzantine Empire article, and the city is the subject of Constantinople.

contentSections.title: Names and Identity
paragraphs: They called themselves Rhomaioi — Romans. Not the heirs of the Romans, not a successor people, but Romans, in an unbroken line from Augustus, ruling the Roman state from the city Constantine had founded as New Rome. Their empire was the Basileia ton Rhomaion, the empire of the Romans, and it is the single most important fact about how they saw themselves.

Nobody in Constantinople ever called themselves a Byzantine. The word is a modern coinage: the German scholar Hieronymus Wolf introduced it in 1557 in his Corpus Historiae Byzantinae, borrowing the name of the small Greek colony of Byzantion that had stood on the site before 330, and later historians found it a convenient way to file the eastern empire separately from Rome. Every person in this article would have rejected the label, and most would not have understood it.

In their own time the disputed word was Greek. Westerners called them Graeci and their ruler the emperor of the Greeks, which was a deliberate denial of the Roman claim, since Latin Christendom had its own emperor of the Romans from 800. The insult ran both ways: when Liutprand of Cremona came as Otto I's ambassador in 968, Nikephoros II Phokas told him that the westerners were not Romans but Lombards. Graikos was a word the Byzantines occasionally used of their language and rarely of themselves; the Arabs and then the Ottomans called them Rum, a name that outlived them in Rumelia and in the Sultanate of Rum.

So why two articles, when the Byzantines were Romans and said so? Because by the seventh century the Latin west and the Greek east had become different cultural worlds — different languages of worship and government, different legal practice, different relations between emperor and church. Separating them is a filing decision about culture, not a verdict on the claim: the page called Romans, which covers the Latin-speaking populations of the former western empire, is the other half of the same story.

contentSections.title: Greek, Latin and the language of the state
paragraphs: The eastern empire began as a Latin state governing a Greek-speaking population, and the gap closed from the top down. Justinian's Digest and Code were issued in Latin in the 530s, but the Novels that followed were mostly published in Greek, because that was what his subjects actually spoke.

The change became formal in the seventh century. Heraclius took the Greek title basileus in 629 in place of the Latin imperial style, and Latin faded from the chancery, the coinage and the army over the following decades. What survived was vocabulary: Greek documents kept Latin words for offices, taxes and military ranks long after anyone could decline them.

The Greek that resulted was two languages at once. Educated writers used a deliberately archaising literary Greek modelled on Attic authors a thousand years dead, while everyone including the educated spoke a living vernacular. A Byzantine historian writing about Turks might call them Persians because that is what a classical model required, which is a recurring problem for anyone reading these sources for facts.

contentSections.title: Roman law in Greek dress
paragraphs: Law was the strongest of the Byzantines' claims to be Roman, and they maintained it as a working system rather than a memory. Justinian's commission produced the Code, the Digest, the Institutes and the Novels between 529 and 534, gathering a millennium of Roman jurisprudence into a usable body.

It was then repeatedly rebuilt for a Greek-speaking society. The Ecloga of 741, issued under Leo III, was a short practical handbook in Greek, with a revised law of marriage and inheritance and a penal system that substituted mutilation for many capital sentences. The Basilika, completed under Leo VI around the end of the ninth century, translated and reorganised the whole Justinianic inheritance into sixty books of Greek.

Alongside the imperial codes ran more local material, such as the Farmer's Law, a collection dealing with village disputes over animals, boundaries and theft that shows a world of free peasant communities rather than great estates. Taken together these texts are why a Byzantine judge in the eleventh century was administering recognisably Roman law, and why western lawyers rediscovering the Digest at Bologna were recovering something the east had never put down. The line ran to the end: Constantine Harmenopoulos compiled the Hexabiblos at Thessalonica in 1345, digesting the whole tradition into six books that Greek courts were still using in the nineteenth century.

contentSections.title: Orthodoxy and the shape of the church
paragraphs: Byzantine religion was Chalcedonian Orthodoxy, organised around the five ancient patriarchates and the seven ecumenical councils, with the patriarch of Constantinople as the senior bishop of the east. After the Arab conquests took Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem out of imperial control in the seventh century, Constantinople was in practice the only patriarchate the emperor could reach, which concentrated religious authority in his capital.

Emperor and church were understood to work as symphonia, a harmony of two powers with distinct spheres. In practice emperors summoned councils, appointed and deposed patriarchs and legislated on doctrine, and the church acquired its independence chiefly through the monasteries, which were wealthy, popular and difficult to coerce.

The rupture with Rome was slow and mutual. The Photian schism of the 860s, the excommunications exchanged in 1054, and the sack of Constantinople in 1204 each widened it, and the attempted reunions at Lyon in 1274 and Florence in 1439 were rejected by most of the Byzantine clergy and population. The last serious internal argument, over the hesychast monks' claim to experience the uncreated light of God directly, was settled in favour of Gregory Palamas at a council in 1351.
Orthodoxy was the Byzantines' primary badge of belonging, more reliably than language and far more than descent.

contentSections.title: Iconoclasm and the broken image
paragraphs: Between 726 and 787, and again from 815 to 843, the Byzantines fought over whether images of Christ and the saints could be venerated at all. The argument was theological — whether an image of Christ claimed to depict the undepictable divine nature — and it was fought with depositions, exiles, beatings and the destruction of art.

It was also a fight about who decided. Emperors led the iconoclast policy and monks led the resistance, and the two women who ended each phase, Irene at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 and Theodora in 843, did so partly by rebuilding alliances with the monasteries. The restoration of 843 is still commemorated in the Orthodox calendar as the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

The result was a settled theory of the image that shaped everything the Byzantines made afterwards: an icon is not a portrait but a channel of honour passing to the person represented, which is why Byzantine religious art is deliberately conventional rather than naturalistic. The losses are permanent — very little religious figural art from before 726 survives inside the empire — and the survivors, such as the icons at Saint Catherine's on Sinai, are mostly those that were outside imperial reach.

contentSections.title: The themes and provincial society
paragraphs: The theme system reorganised the provinces around the army after the seventh-century catastrophes, and in doing so it reorganised society. Soldiers were settled on land that carried an obligation of military service, so that a province supported and produced its own troops instead of paying for a distant field army.

That created a broad class of soldier-farmers holding land in return for service, and a provincial world of villages that paid tax collectively and dealt with the state through their own headmen. The Farmer's Law describes exactly this society, arguing about strayed oxen and damaged vines.

It was eroded by success. As the frontier moved away from the interior, powerful provincial families — the dynatoi — bought out peasant holdings, and the tenth-century emperors legislated against them repeatedly because every village absorbed into a magnate's estate was a soldier and a taxpayer lost. Basil II made the wealthy liable for their poorer neighbours' unpaid tax, a measure abandoned soon after his death in 1025. The military smallholding did not survive the eleventh century, and the empire increasingly hired its soldiers instead.

contentSections.title: Ceremony and the idea of order
paragraphs: The Byzantines believed that the empire mirrored the order of heaven, and that maintaining correct order — taxis — was a religious duty rather than a courtly affectation. Ceremony performed that belief, and it was documented with extraordinary care.

Constantine VII compiled the Book of Ceremonies in the tenth century precisely because he thought the imperial order was decaying into disorder, and the result records processions, acclamations, receptions and the correct dress and words for each. Liutprand of Cremona, an unfriendly witness, describes mechanical golden lions that roared and a throne that rose towards the ceiling during his audience — stagecraft aimed at ambassadors from places with nothing comparable.

The same instinct governed dealings abroad. Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio, written privately for his son, explains which neighbours to bribe, which to set against each other and what to say when a barbarian ruler asks for imperial regalia or an imperial bride. Diplomacy, ceremony and theology were one subject, and the Byzantines were better at it than anyone around them for several centuries.

contentSections.title: Eunuchs, families and women at court
paragraphs: Byzantine society had a distinctive institution in the court eunuch. Eunuchs were barred from the throne and therefore trusted with everything else: they held the highest household offices, commanded armies and occupied the patriarchate, and families sometimes had a son castrated as a career decision. Narses, who commanded the armies that finished the Gothic War in Italy, is the best-known example.

Women of the elite lived formally secluded and were nonetheless conspicuous in politics. Irene ruled in her own name from 797 to 802, Theodora ended the second iconoclasm as regent in 843, and Zoe transmitted the imperial title through three marriages in the eleventh century. Property rights in the Justinianic tradition gave women real control over dowries and inheritance, which is a large part of why imperial women could act politically at all.

The most articulate voice is Anna Komnene, daughter of Alexios I, who after failing to take the throne for her husband retired to a monastery and wrote the Alexiad, a history of her father's reign. It is the only major medieval history by a woman in Greek and one of the sharpest accounts anyone wrote of the crusaders' arrival.

contentSections.title: The classical inheritance
paragraphs: Almost all surviving ancient Greek literature reaches the modern world through Byzantine copies, and this was a matter of deliberate effort rather than luck. Schooling for the elite was built on the classical authors, and a career in the civil service required the ability to write in their style.

The ninth century saw the decisive work. The change to minuscule script made copying faster and cheaper and prompted a wave of transcription from older manuscripts, and Photios, patriarch and scholar, compiled the Bibliotheca, a set of notes on hundreds of books he had read — many of which are now lost, so that his summaries are all that remains of them. The Suda, a tenth-century encyclopaedia, preserves a comparable mass of quotation and fact.

The tradition of learning continued to the end. Michael Psellos wrote philosophy, history and gossip in the eleventh century and revived the study of Plato; a law school was refounded at Constantinople in 1045; and in the empire's final century scholars such as Manuel Chrysoloras carried Greek texts and Greek teaching to Italy, where they fed directly into the Renaissance.

contentSections.title: Icons, ivory and enamel
paragraphs: Byzantine art was made for use rather than for display, and its prestige media were small and expensive. Ivory triptychs such as the Harbaville Triptych in the Louvre, carved at Constantinople in the tenth century, folded shut for private devotion; cloisonné enamel set saints in gold on reliquaries and book covers; and silk woven under imperial control was a diplomatic gift as much as a fabric.

Monumental art meant mosaic, and the technique was pushed further here than anywhere else. Gold tesserae were set at slight angles so that the background shifts as the viewer moves, and faces were modelled in tiny graded cubes, as in the Deesis in Hagia Sophia that leads this article.

Byzantine objects travelled further than Byzantine armies. Enamels and silks reached western treasuries as gifts and as loot, the great hoard taken in 1204 ending up largely at San Marco in Venice, and Byzantine models shaped church decoration from Kyiv to Sicily. Painters in Italy were still working in the Byzantine manner in the thirteenth century, which is why the period immediately before Giotto is conventionally called the maniera greca.

contentSections.title: The commonwealth abroad
paragraphs: The most durable Byzantine export was not territory but a religious and political model. Cyril and Methodius were sent to Moravia in 863 and devised an alphabet for Slavic, and the mission's descendants — the Cyrillic script named after Cyril — carried liturgy, law and literature in a language the converts could use.

Bulgaria's ruler Boris accepted Christianity from Constantinople in 864, and in 988 Vladimir of Kiev was baptised and married an emperor's sister, bringing the Rus' into the same religious world. The envoys' report in the Primary Chronicle, that at worship in Hagia Sophia they did not know whether they stood in heaven or on earth, is a Rus' account of a Byzantine service written down over a century later, and should be read as a conversion narrative rather than a transcript.

What resulted was a group of states sharing Orthodox Christianity, Byzantine liturgy, Byzantine legal borrowings and an imperial vocabulary, while remaining politically independent and often at war with the empire. Bulgarian and Serbian rulers took the title of emperor themselves, and after 1453 Moscow argued that it had inherited the position outright.

contentSections.title: Who counted as a Roman
paragraphs: Byzantine identity was joinable, which is why it lasted through repeated catastrophe. The test was Orthodox Christianity, the Greek language and obedience to the emperor, and a family that met those conditions was Roman regardless of where it had come from two generations earlier.

The elite shows this plainly. Armenians were so numerous among generals and emperors that several dynasties were of Armenian origin, including that of Basil I; Slavs settled across the Balkans from the sixth century were absorbed over time; Leo III came from Syria; and Turkish, Norman and Scandinavian soldiers served in the armies and their descendants disappear into the population.

The limits are equally clear. A miaphysite Christian in Egypt or Syria was not fully inside this community even before the Arab conquests removed those provinces, and the argument over the nature of Christ was also an argument about who belonged. In the last centuries, as the empire shrank to a Greek-speaking rump, some writers began using Hellene as a term of pride in a way that would have sounded pagan to their ancestors — a late shift, and not the beginning of modern Greek nationalism, which is a nineteenth-century development.

contentSections.title: After 1453
paragraphs: The people did not end when the city fell. Mehmed II installed a patriarch and organised the Orthodox population of his empire as a self-governing religious community, which preserved the church, its courts and its schools under Ottoman rule, and its members went on being called Rum — Romans — in Turkish.

Some of the elite went west. Scholars carrying Greek manuscripts had been arriving in Italy for decades before 1453 and more followed, and their teaching gave western Europe access to Greek texts it had known only at second hand. Others rose inside the Ottoman system, and Greek families from the Phanar district of Constantinople supplied the sultans with interpreters and provincial governors for centuries.

The claim to Rome outlived the claimants. The Ottoman sultan styled himself Kayser-i Rum, Caesar of the Romans; Moscow developed the argument that it was a third Rome after the first and second had fallen; and ordinary Greek-speakers in the Ottoman lands went on calling themselves Romioi into the twentieth century. The word Byzantine, meanwhile, was still nearly a century away from being invented.

timeline.title: The west ends and the east does not
timeline.description: With no emperor left in Italy, the Roman state and the people who called themselves Romans continue from Constantinople alone.

timeline.title: The baptism of the Rus'
timeline.description: Vladimir of Kiev converts and marries an emperor's sister, bringing the Rus' lands into the Orthodox world.

timeline.title: Mutual excommunications
timeline.description: Legates from Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate one another, hardening a separation that had been growing for two centuries.

timeline.title: The Latin occupation
timeline.description: The Fourth Crusade takes Constantinople and installs a western regime, scattering the Byzantine elite into successor states in exile.

timeline.title: The city recovered
timeline.description: Michael VIII retakes Constantinople; the Deesis mosaic in Hagia Sophia is usually dated to the years just after.

timeline.title: Hesychasm vindicated
timeline.description: A council at Constantinople upholds Gregory Palamas and the monks' claim to experience the uncreated light of God directly.

timeline.title: Union rejected at home
timeline.description: The union agreed at Florence is repudiated by most Byzantine clergy and laity, who prefer Ottoman rule to Latin terms.

timeline.title: The city falls
timeline.description: Mehmed II takes Constantinople; the Orthodox population is reorganised as a religious community that the Ottomans go on calling Rum.

timeline.title: The name Byzantine is invented
timeline.description: Hieronymus Wolf publishes his Corpus Historiae Byzantinae, giving modern scholarship a label that nobody in the empire had ever used.

sectionImages.caption: An icon of Christ being whitewashed with a sponge on a pole, set beside the sponge offered at the Crucifixion, in the Chludov Psalter of about 850 to 875.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan illuminator
sectionImages.source: State Historical Museum, Moscow (MS D.129), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Made within a generation of the restoration of images in 843, and openly polemical: the painter puts the whitewashing of an icon directly below the soldiers at the Crucifixion so that the two sponges rhyme, equating iconoclasts with Christ's tormentors. The figure with the pole is usually identified as John the Grammarian, the iconoclast patriarch deposed in 843. It is evidence for how the winning side wanted the quarrel remembered rather than a neutral record of it. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: Ceremony and the idea of order
sectionImages.caption: The Barberini ivory, carved at Constantinople in the first half of the sixth century, showing a mounted emperor with a conquered barbarian reaching up to his spear.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan ivory carver; photographed by Marie-Lan Nguyen
sectionImages.date: first half of the 6th century; photographed 2011
sectionImages.source: Musée du Louvre, Paris (OA 9063), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Four of an original five ivory panels survive; the missing leaf would have balanced the officer on the left. The emperor is most often identified as Anastasius I or Justinian I, and neither identification is secure, since the panel carries no inscription naming him. Christ blesses from the top panel while defeated peoples bring tribute below, which is the imperial idea of order set out in a single object: victory, tribute and divine approval arranged in tiers. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: A hunter on the floor mosaic of the Great Palace at Constantinople, laid in the sixth century. It is one of the few Byzantine images of ordinary people at work rather than of saints or emperors.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan mosaicists
sectionImages.source: Great Palace Mosaic Museum, Istanbul, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The pavement ran round a peristyle courtyard of the imperial palace and was excavated from 1935. It carries hunters, herdsmen, children, farm animals and mythological beasts with no Christian subject anywhere, which is why it is usually read as a late antique inheritance rather than a Byzantine invention; the Commons file dates it to the fifth century, while most scholars now place it in the sixth. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: A gold histamenon of Nikephoros II Phokas, struck at Constantinople between 963 and 969, with Christ on one face and the emperor crowned by the Virgin on the other.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan die-cutter; photographed by Classical Numismatic Group
sectionImages.source: Classical Numismatic Group, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: This is the emperor who told Liutprand of Cremona in 968 that the westerners were not Romans but Lombards. The legends are Greek and the imagery is Christian, and both sat on a coin that circulated as the money of the Roman state: the claim in this section travelled across the Mediterranean in this form for centuries. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.5.

sectionImages.section: Greek, Latin and the language of the state
sectionImages.caption: The opening miniature of a chrysobull issued in Greek by Andronikos II in 1301, in which the emperor hands the document to Christ.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan illuminator
sectionImages.source: Byzantine and Christian Museum, Athens, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Four sheets of vellum glued into a roll, confirming and extending privileges granted to Nikolaos, metropolitan of Monemvasia, and signed by the emperor himself in red ink. The chancery had worked in Greek since the seventh century, but its vocabulary stayed Latin: the offices, taxes and ranks such a document names are Roman words in Greek dress. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: A page of Constantine Harmenopoulos's Hexabiblos, the last great Byzantine law book, in a manuscript copied in 1359.
sectionImages.creator: Constantine Harmenopoulos; copied by an unknown Greek scribe
sectionImages.source: Biblioteca Marciana, Venice (Gr. 183, fol. 104r), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Harmenopoulos was a judge at Thessalonica who reduced the Basilika and its commentaries to six books of working law. The copy here was made fourteen years after he finished it; the same text was printed repeatedly under Ottoman rule and was still cited in Greek courts in the nineteenth century, which makes it the longest-lived Roman law book anywhere. Public domain.

sectionImages.section: Orthodoxy and the shape of the church
sectionImages.caption: The katholikon of the Great Lavra on Mount Athos, founded in 963 and rebuilt many times since, photographed in 2006.
sectionImages.creator: Photographed by Dimboukas
sectionImages.note: Athanasios the Athonite founded the Lavra with money and a charter from Nikephoros II, and it is the oldest of the twenty ruling monasteries of Athos. Houses like this are where the church's independence actually lay: wealthy, self-governing, popular, and difficult for an emperor to coerce, as the iconoclast and hesychast quarrels both showed. The red wash and much of the present fabric are later. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The lead seal of a judge of the Drougoubitai, a Slav people settled inside the empire near Thessalonica, struck in the eighth century.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Byzantine engraver; photographed by Classical Numismatic Group
sectionImages.source: Classical Numismatic Group, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: A bust of the archangel Michael on one face, five lines of Greek naming the office on the other, and two holes where the cord ran through the document it closed. Seals are the main evidence for provincial administration because the documents themselves are almost all lost. The dealer's catalogue dated this one to the seventh century; the Commons file places it in the eighth. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.5.

sectionImages.section: Eunuchs, families and women at court
sectionImages.caption: The empress Zoe in the south gallery of Hagia Sophia, an eleventh-century mosaic whose imperial heads were reset at least once.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan mosaicist; photographed by Myrabella
sectionImages.source: Hagia Sophia, Istanbul, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Zoe carried the imperial title through three marriages, and the panel was edited to match: the head of the emperor beside her was replaced, the inscription rewritten for Constantine IX, and her own face appears to have been reworked as well. A mosaic altered to keep up with an empress's husbands is as good an image of Byzantine court politics as survives. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: David composing the psalms, attended by a personification of Melody, in the Paris Psalter made at Constantinople about 960.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan illuminator
sectionImages.source: Bibliothèque nationale de France (Grec 139, fol. 1v), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: The seated figures, the labelled personifications and the reclining mountain god at the right are the visual language of Greek and Roman painting, used by a tenth-century Christian workshop about a thousand years after it was invented. Whether such pages copy a lost antique model or reconstruct the manner from study is argued; either way they are deliberate classicism rather than unbroken habit. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The Harbaville Triptych, carved in ivory at Constantinople in the tenth century and opened here to its Deesis and ranks of saints.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Constantinopolitan ivory carver
sectionImages.source: Musée du Louvre, Paris (OA 3247), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: About 24 cm high with hinged wings, made to fold shut and travel with its owner. Traces of gilding and colour survive in the grooves, so the bare ivory look is an accident of age; the piece is the finest of the group of ivories conventionally associated with the court workshops of the Macedonian emperors. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The baptism of Boris of Bulgaria in 864, in a miniature of the Madrid Skylitzes copied in Sicily in the twelfth century.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown illuminator of the Madrid Skylitzes
sectionImages.source: Biblioteca Nacional de España, Madrid (Vitr. 26-2, fol. 68v), via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Boris took the name of the reigning emperor, Michael III, at his baptism, which is exactly how the commonwealth worked: a ruler entered the Byzantine religious order and acquired an imperial godfather without becoming an imperial subject. The manuscript is the only illustrated Greek chronicle to survive, made in Norman Sicily by several hands three centuries after the event. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The lead seal of Ablgharib Artsruni, an Armenian noble serving as a Byzantine vestes and strategos, struck in the third quarter of the eleventh century.
sectionImages.creator: Unknown Byzantine engraver; photographed for the Armenian Numismatic Research Organization
sectionImages.source: Armenian Numismatic Research Organization, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: An Armenian dynastic name, Byzantine court titles and an inscription in Greek on one small disc of lead. Armenians served in such numbers that several imperial dynasties were of Armenian descent, and those who rose in imperial service normally conformed to Chalcedonian orthodoxy — which is the point: the qualification was religion, language and allegiance, not birth. sectionImages.caption: Cardinal Bessarion, the Greek scholar who left his library to Venice, painted about 1473 to 1475 by Justus van Gent and Pedro Berruguete.
sectionImages.creator: Justus van Gent and Pedro Berruguete
sectionImages.source: From the series of Illustrious Men painted for the studiolo at Urbino, via Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.note: Bessarion was born at Trebizond, argued for union with Rome at Florence in 1439, and stayed in Italy as a cardinal when the union was rejected at home. He bequeathed his Greek manuscripts to Venice, where they became the founding collection of the Marciana, and the panel was painted a year or two after his death in 1472. Public domain.
